source_text: Cur ergo dubitemus dicere, quod scriptura non dubitat exprimere? cur haesitabit fidei ueritas, in quo scripturae numquam haesitauit auctoritas? ecce enim Osee prophetes ait ex persona patris: 2am non saluabo eos in arcu, neque in equis, neque in equitibus; sed saluabo eos in domino deo ipsorum. si deus saluare se dicit in deo, non autem saluat nisi in Christo deus, cur ergo homo dubitet Christum deum dicere, quem deum a patre animaduertit positum per scripturas esse? immo si non saluat nisi in deo pater deus, saluari non poterit a deo patre quisquam, nisi confessus fuerit Christum deum, in quo se et per quem se repromittit pater salutem daturum; ut merito quisquis illum agnoscit esse deum, salutem inueniat in deo Christo; quisquis non recognoscit esse deum, salutem perdiderit, quoniam alibi nisi in Christo deo eam inuenire non poterit. Quo modo enim Esaias: ecce uirgo concipiet et pariet jilium, et uocabitis nomen eius Emmanuel, quod interpretatum est nobiscum deus, sic Christus ipse dicit: ecce ego uobiscum sum usque ad consummationem saecule, deus, immo multo magis etiam in nobis est. nobiscum est Christus: est ergo cuius nomen est nobiscum deus, quia et nobiscum est. aut numquid non est nobiscum? quo modo ergo dicit se nobiscum esse? est ergo nobiscum: sed § quoniam nobiscum est, Emmanuel, id est, nobiscum deus, dictus est. deus ergo quia nobiscum est, nobiscum deus dictus est. idem prophetes: conualescite, manus dissolutae, et genua debilia; consolamini pusillanimes sensu, conualescite, nolite timere: ecce deus noster iudicium retribuet: ipse ueniet et saluabit nos: tunc aperientur oculi caecorum, et aures surdorum audient; tunc saliet claudus sicut ceruus, et diserta erit lingua mutorum. si in aduentu dei dicit prophetes haec futura signa, quae facta sunt, aut dei filium agnoscant Christum, in cuius aduentu et a quo haec sanitatum signa facta sunt: aut diuinitatis Christi ueritate superati, in alteram haeresim ruentes, Christum dum filium dei et deum confiteri nolunt, patrem illum esse confiteantur. uocibus enim prophetarum inclusi iam Christum deum negare non possunt. quid ergo respondent, cum in aduentu dei haec signa futura dicuntur, quae in aduentu Christi gesta sunt? Christum qualiter accipiunt deum (deum enim iam negare non possunt), qua patrem aut qua filium? si qua filium, cur dei filium deum negant? si qua patrem, cur eos non sequuntur, qui eiusmodi blasphemias tenere uidentur? nisi quoniam nobis in hoc aduersus illos de ueritate certamine hoc interim sufficit, ut quocumque genere conuicti Christum confiteantur et deum, quem etiam deum negare uoluerunt. Per Abacuc prophetam ait: deus ab Africo ueniet et sanctus de monte opaco et condenso. quem uolunt isti ab Africo uenire? Si uenisse aiunt omnipotentem deum patrem, ergo de loco deus pater uenit, ex quo etiam loco cluditur, et intra sedis alicuius angustias continetur; et iam per istos, ut diximus, Sabelliana haeresis sacrilega corporatur, siquidem Christus non filius sed pater creditur: et nouo more, dum ab istis destricte homo nudus asseritur, per eos rursum Christus pater deus omnipotens comprobatur. at si in Bethlehem, cuius metaturae regio ad meridianam respicit plagam caeli, Christus nascitur, qui per scripturas et deus dicitur, merito deus hic ab Africo uenire describitur, quia a Bethlehem uenturus esse praeuide- ’ batur. eligant ergo ex duobus quid uelint hunc, qui ab Africo uenit,—filium esse, an patrem: deus enim dicitur ab Africo uenturus. si filium, quid dubitant Christum et deum dicere? deum enim scriptura dicit esse uenturum. si patrem, quid dubitant cum Sabellii temeritate misceri, qui Christum patrem dicit? nisi quoniam, siue illum patrem siue filium dixerint, ab haeresi sua inuiti licet desciscant necesse est, qui Christum hominem tantummodo solent dicere, dum illum, rebus ipsis coacti, deum incipiunt promere, siue dum illum patrem, siue dum illum filium uoluerint nuncupare.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore why do we doubt to say what scripture does not doubt to express? Why will the truth of faith hesitate, in which the authority of scriptures has never hesitated? For behold the prophet Hosea says in the person of the Father: I will save them not in the bow, nor in horses, nor in horsemen, but I will save them in the Lord their God. If God says He will save in God, and yet God does not save except in Christ, why therefore does man doubt to call Christ God, whom God the Father has noted through scriptures to be? Indeed if the Father God does not save except in God, no one will be able to be saved by God the Father unless he has confessed Christ to be God, in whom and through whom the Father promises to give salvation; so that deservedly whoever acknowledges Him to be God may find salvation in God Christ; whoever does not recognize Him to be God will have lost salvation, because he cannot find it anywhere else except in Christ God. How indeed Isaiah says: Behold a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and you will call His name Emmanuel, which is interpreted as God with us, so Christ Himself says: Behold I am with you until the end of the age, God, or even more so He is in us. Christ is with us: therefore He is the one whose name is God with us, because He is with us. Or does He not exist with us? How therefore does He say that He exists with us? Therefore He exists with us: but since He exists with us, He is called Emmanuel, that is, God with us. Therefore God, because He exists with us, is called God with us. The same prophet says: Be strong, you with weakened hands, and you with feeble knees; be comforted, you fainthearted, be strong, do not fear: behold our God will repay judgment: He Himself will come and save us: then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will hear; then the lame will leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute will speak. If the prophet says that these signs will occur at the coming of God, which have been done, either they acknowledge Christ the Son of God, in whose coming and from whom these signs of healing have been done: or overcome by the truth of Christ's divinity, they fall into another heresy, not wanting to confess Christ as the Son of God and God. For they can no longer deny Christ to be God, enclosed as they are by the words of the prophets. What therefore do they respond, when these signs are said to be future at the coming of God, which have been done at the coming of Christ? How do they receive Christ as God (for they can no longer deny God), as Father or as Son? If as Son, why do they deny the Son of God to be God? If as Father, why do they not follow those who seem to hold such blasphemies? Unless indeed it is enough for us in this contest of truth against them, that meanwhile they confess Christ to be God, whom they also wanted to deny as God. Through the prophet Habakkuk it is said: God will come from Africa and the Holy One from the dark and dense mountain. Whom do they want to come from Africa? If they say that the omnipotent Father God has come, therefore God the Father comes from a place, from which He is also enclosed, and contained within the narrowness of some seat; and already through them, as we have said, the sacrilegious Sabellian heresy is formed, since Christ is believed to be not the Son but the Father: and in a new manner, while they assert that man is naked and separate from God, through them Christ is again proven to be the omnipotent Father God. But if Christ, who is said through scriptures to be God, is born in Bethlehem, whose region lies towards the southern part of the sky, deservedly God is described as coming from Africa, because it was foreseen that He would come from Bethlehem. Let them therefore choose from two options what they want this one, who comes from Africa, to be—either the Son or the Father: for God is said to come from Africa. If the Son, why do they doubt to call Christ God? For scripture says that God is coming. If the Father, why do they doubt to be mixed with the temerity of Sabellius, who says that Christ is the Father? Unless indeed, whether they call Him Father or Son, they must descend from their heresy, though unwilling, who are accustomed to call Christ only a man, while they begin to proclaim Him God, either when they want to name Him Father or when they want to name Him Son.

choices.english: contained within the narrowness of some seat
choices.why: part of the argument against the Sabellian view

pass_b_english: Why do we hesitate to say what Scripture clearly states? The authority of Scripture has never wavered, so why should the truth of our faith be any different? The prophet Hosea, speaking on behalf of the Father, says, 'I will save them, not with bows or horses or horsemen, but in the Lord their God' (Hosea 2:18). If God saves us in Himself, and this salvation comes through Christ, then why do people doubt that Christ is God? After all, Scripture makes it clear that Christ is the one through whom God saves us. In fact, the Father promises to give us salvation through Christ, so if we don't acknowledge Christ as God, we can't receive salvation from the Father. This means that recognizing Christ as God is essential to finding salvation in Him, and those who refuse to do so will lose out on salvation because it can't be found anywhere else. The prophet Isaiah announces the birth of a son, saying, 'He will be called Emmanuel, which means God with us' (Isaiah 7:14). Similarly, Christ Himself says, 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age,' and He is not just with us, but in us. Since Christ is the one who is with us, His name is rightly understood as 'God with us.' He is, in fact, the embodiment of God's presence with us. The same prophet encourages the weak and fearful, saying, 'Be strong, do not fear; our God will come and save us.' And when God comes, the blind will see, the deaf will hear, and the lame will leap - all of which happened when Christ came. So, either those who deny Christ's divinity must acknowledge Him as the Son of God who brought these healings, or they must admit that they are abandoning their heresy and embracing the truth about Christ's divinity. The words of the prophets have them cornered, and they can no longer deny that Christ is God. The question is, how do they receive Christ as God - as the Father or as the Son? If they see Him as the Son, why do they refuse to call Him God? And if they see Him as the Father, why don't they follow the logic of Sabellius, who believes that Christ is the Father? Perhaps, in the end, it's enough that they are forced to confess Christ as God, even if they initially tried to deny it. The prophet Habakkuk says, 'God will come from Africa, and the Holy One from the dark and dense mountain' (Habakkuk 3:3). Who do they think is coming from Africa? If they say it's the omnipotent Father, then they're implying that the Father is limited to a particular place and can be contained. This would be a form of the Sabellian heresy, which confuses Christ with the Father. On the other hand, if Christ is the one who comes from Africa, and Scripture says that God is coming from Africa, then why do they doubt that Christ is God? They need to choose: is the one coming from Africa the Son or the Father? Either way, they're forced to acknowledge Christ's divinity, whether they like it or not.

review.notes: Pass B fails on completeness and accuracy regarding the final argument. The Latin text concludes with a complex conditional regarding the heretics' descent from their error: 'nisi quoniam, siue illum patrem siue filium dixerint, ab haeresi sua inuiti licet desciscant necesse est, qui Christum hominem tantummodo solent dicere, dum illum, rebus ipsis coacti, deum incipiunt promere, siue dum illum patrem, siue dum illum filium uoluerint nuncupare.' Pass A captures this nuance (that they are forced by things themselves to begin to proclaim Him God when they name Him Father or Son). Pass B omits the specific detail that they are 'accustomed to call Christ only a man' (qui Christum hominem tantummodo solent dicere) and simplifies the conclusion to 'they're forced to acknowledge Christ's divinity, whether they like it or not', losing the specific causal mechanism of their reluctant transition from seeing Him as 'only a man' to naming Him 'Father or Son'.
reasons: Pass B omits the clause 'qui Christum hominem tantummodo solent dicere' (who are accustomed to call Christ only a man) and the specific distinction that they begin to proclaim Him God specifically when they attempt to name Him either Father or Son, which is central to the author's point about their reluctant shift from human-only Christology.
